title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
oneLiner: SQL injection's cousin in the browser: user input that ends up running as code in someone else's page.
keyTakeaway: Treat everything users submit as text, never as HTML. Encode it for the place it's going (React does this automatically for anything in {curly braces}); be very suspicious of dangerouslySetInnerHTML, innerHTML and anything else that turns a string into markup; and add a Content Security Policy as a second line of defense.
explanation:
A comment box saves what you type and shows it to everyone who opens the page. If the page builds its HTML by pasting the saved comment straight in, then a comment containing HTML becomes part of the page -- including tags that run JavaScript, like an image with a broken src and an onerror handler. That script runs in every reader's browser, on your site, as them. It can read what the page shows, act with their session, or replace the page with a fake login form. That's stored cross-site scripting.

The fix is the same idea as parameterized SQL: keep data and code apart. When user text goes into HTML, encode it so `<` becomes `<` and so on; the browser then displays the characters instead of interpreting them. Toggle escaping in the demo and replay the attacks. Modern frameworks do this by default: React escapes any value you render with {curly braces}, and Razor in ASP.NET encodes @values. You only get XSS when you go around them -- dangerouslySetInnerHTML in React, @Html.Raw in Razor, element.innerHTML in plain JavaScript -- or when user input lands in a URL attribute: React still renders href={userUrl} with a javascript: URL, so allow only http and https links. If you truly need user-supplied formatting, run it through a sanitizer library that keeps a small allowlist of tags.

A Content Security Policy (CSP) header is the backstop: it tells the browser which scripts the page is allowed to run (for example, only files from your own domain, never inline handlers like onerror). Even if an injection slips through, the browser refuses to run it.

About the demo: the "victim's page" is a sandboxed frame, so the injected script really runs, but it is cut off from this app and its session token is fake.
